claims.claim: QUEL was the Ingres query language; syntax `range of e is employee` / `retrieve (e.name, e.dept) where e.salary > 10000`

citations.quote:
range of s is student
append to s (name = "philip", age = 17, sex = "m", state = "FL")

retrieve (s.all) where s.state = "FL"

claims.notes: This is not a verbatim historical example, but it is syntactically valid, idiomatic QUEL: declare a tuple variable with 'range of <var> is <relation>', then 'retrieve (<target list>) where <qualification>', exactly matching the shown pattern with a different table/column names. The Wikipedia QUEL page and Ingres/Actian's own QUEL reference guide confirm this general form.

citations.quote: The design of POSTGRES | Proceedings of the 1986 ACM SIGMOD international conference on Management of data

claims.notes: Confirmed: authors Michael Stonebraker and Lawrence A. Rowe, in Proceedings of the 1986 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, pp. 340-355.

claims.claim: POSTQUEL time-travel syntax `retrieve (e.salary) from e in emp["1985"]`

citations.quote: To find the salary of Sam at time T, one would query: retrieve (EMP.salary) from EMP [T] where EMP.name = "Sam"

claims.notes: The real POSTQUEL time-travel syntax bracket-qualifies the relation name directly (e.g. 'EMP [T]' or 'EMP["1980"]'), not a separately-declared range variable referenced as 'from e in emp[...]' — POSTQUEL (like QUEL) declares range variables with a separate 'range of' statement, and time-travel brackets attach to the relation reference itself. The later hybrid-SQL time-travel syntax in early Postgres (v6.x, before SQL retrieve was even 'SELECT') used single-quoted bounds like cities['epoch','now'], not a bare year string in double quotes. The film's `retrieve (e.salary) from e in emp["1985"]` mixes an Ingres/QUEL-style inline 'from x in y' idiom (not actually used this way in POSTQUEL) with a made-up bracket literal.
claims.on_screen_fix: Use `range of e is emp\nretrieve (e.salary) where e = e["1985"]` style, or simply show the attested SQL-era form `SELECT salary FROM emp['1985']` labeled explicitly as illustrative/simplified, or cite the documented example: `retrieve (EMP.salary) from EMP[T] where EMP.name = "Sam"`.

claims.claim: Postgres95 "terminal monitor" / `monitor` program

citations.quote: fprintf(stdout,"Welcome to the POSTGRES95 terminal monitor\n");
A new program (psql) was provided for interactive SQL queries, which used GNU Readline. This largely superseded the old monitor program.

claims.notes: The 'Postgres95 terminal monitor' banner string is verbatim in src/bin/monitor/monitor.c of the Postgres95 1.01 virgin-sources commit (d31084e9), viewable on the public GitHub mirror. Note the nuance: the underlying 'monitor' program itself predates Postgres95 (inherited from Berkeley POSTGRES) and was soon superseded within Postgres95's own lifetime by psql — but the exact string 'POSTGRES95 terminal monitor' is real and shipped.

claims.claim: Slonik = Russian for "little elephant"; mascot from 1997

citations.quote: The PostgreSQL logo is an elephant, known as "Slonik".
David Yang, a community member, suggested making an elephant the mascot in 1997.

claims.notes: 'Slonik' (слоник) is indeed a Russian diminutive for 'little elephant'; translation is correct. The elephant-as-mascot idea was proposed in April 1997 (pgsql-hackers), matching the claim.

claims.claim: "because elephants remember" (reason for the elephant, David Yang 1997 proposal)

citations.quote: but if you want an animal-based logo, how about some sort of elephant? After all, as the Agatha Christie title read, elephants can remember
[...] but if you want an animal-based logo, how about some sort of elephant? After all, as the Agatha Christie title read, elephants can remember ... — Yang

claims.notes: David Yang's actual April 3, 1997 message (quoted on the official PostgreSQL wiki) says 'elephants can remember', referencing Agatha Christie's novel title 'Elephants Can Remember' — not the more famous 'elephants never forget' framing. The primary archive link (archives.postgresql.org/pgsql-hackers/1997-04/msg00094.php) is now dead/404, so this rests on the PostgreSQL wiki's own quoted excerpt plus the LearnSQL retelling, which agree with each other.
claims.on_screen_fix: If quoting Yang directly, use 'elephants can remember' (Agatha Christie reference), not 'elephants never forget'.

claims.claim: "because elephants remember" as the reason for the elephant

citations.quote: how about some sort of elephant? After all, as the Agatha Christie title read, elephants can remember ... — Yang

claims.notes: As scoped in the ledger (reason for choosing an elephant, not for the specific name 'Slonik'), this is accurate: Yang's 1997 proposal cites the 'elephants remember' association. Separately, per the Habr Postgres Pro retrospective, the specific filename/name 'Slonik' (slonik.gif) was reportedly just a Russian-language filename habit of a designer (Ekaterina Papchinskaya) and stuck by convention, not chosen for a 'remembers' pun — so 'elephants remember' explains the animal choice, not the Slonik name itself. A separate, later (1998) contributor, Dan Delaney, is the one on record with the fuller 'big, strong, reliable, and never forgets' phrasing — don't attribute that fuller quote to Yang/1997.
